citation.title: Reply to Nick Cammarata's announcement of 'Neural Networks Are Already Clean' (post on X)

verification_method: Fetched 2026-10-20. A direct WebFetch of x.com returned HTTP 402. The post was retrieved through two independent public mirror APIs (fxtwitter and vxtwitter) with curl; both returned byte-identical post text, the same author record (display name 'Leo Gao', handle nabla_theta, bio mentioning 'scaling SAEs to GPT-4'), the same timestamp (Thu Oct 15 22:35:12 +0000 2026) and the same parent (a post by @nickcammarata, id 2110757819427574056). The full text is quoted below; it is the entire post.

claims.planned: Gao's critique: an explanation that cannot be used to simulate the neuron has not really explained it; the field is evaluating explanations by vibes; simulation is harder than finding plausible explanations
claims.finding: This is the complete text of the post.
claims.quote:
this is cool work, but i think people are overupdating on how optimistic to be about interp.

in particular, we need to more rigorously evaluate explanations, rather than just going off vibes. imo if you can't simulate a neuron you haven't really explained it. my guess is simulating the neurons is way harder than finding plausible explanations. I have a post on this in the works.

(i know the blog talks argues simulations are bad, but i think all of the downsides described are avoided by looking at KL instead of neuron correlation.)

claims.planned: The roadmap's phrasing, 'an explanation that cannot predict a neuron's activations on held-out data has not been demonstrated', is a quote from Gao
claims.finding: That sentence does not appear in the post. It is a paraphrase. The closest verified wording is 'imo if you can't simulate a neuron you haven't really explained it.' The course quotes the verified wording and attributes the paraphrase to the roadmap, not to Gao.
claims.quote: imo if you can't simulate a neuron you haven't really explained it.

claims.planned: Gao's proposed fix for the essay's objections to simulation scoring is to score by KL divergence rather than activation correlation
claims.finding: Stated in the parenthetical. The post does not spell out the KL procedure; the natural reading, consistent with the ablation-style scoring in Bills et al. 2023 (Jensen-Shannon divergence after replacing the neuron with its simulation) and the downstream-KL metric in Gao et al. 2024, is: substitute the simulated activations into the model and measure the divergence of the output distribution from the original.
claims.quote: (i know the blog talks argues simulations are bad, but i think all of the downsides described are avoided by looking at KL instead of neuron correlation.)

claims.planned: Gao published a longer critique (reported in secondary coverage under the title 'Neural networks are not already clean')
claims.finding: The post says a longer post is 'in the works'. Searches on 2026-10-20 for a LessWrong or blog post by Gao with that title found only a secondary mention in a Substack commentary; the LessWrong linkpost for the essay (posts/x4kvabkF2Jk8GLZp8) has comments from other researchers but no post or comment by Gao was found in its fetched text. Treat the longer piece as not located; do not cite it.
claims.quote: I have a post on this in the works.

teachable_points.point: The disagreement is narrower than the headlines: both sides want held-out prediction. They differ on what the simulator must predict (token-level activation correlation vs effect on the model's output distribution) and on whether a test should be run before or after 'normal science' has produced a story.
teachable_points.quote: all of the downsides described are avoided by looking at KL instead of neuron correlation
